feedback: If a learner expects a reversed cell to still brighten the bulb: the cells push against each other when one faces the opposite way, so the combined push shrinks — the bulb dims, and if two equal cells oppose it goes out. Adding a cell only helps when all the pushes line up the same direction.
If a learner expects brightness to climb forever: too many cells push too much current through the filament and it burns out, so there is a maximum.

If a learner says the extra cell 'refills' or 'tops up' electricity the bulb used: the current flowing into the bulb equals the current flowing out — the current is not used up; energy is passed on to the bulb as light and heat, and the extra cell adds push/energy, not a refill.
Reinforce the fair test: because only the cell count changed while the bulb, wiring and type of cell stayed the same, a clear brightness change is most likely due to the number of cells.
activities.intendedInsight: More cells in series give a bigger combined push (more voltage → a larger current → more energy delivered to the bulb each second), so the bulb glows brighter — but only when the cells line up the same way. Voltage is a push WITH a direction, not just a count of cells, and 'more is brighter' has a real ceiling.
learnerActions: Start with a single cell and one bulb; note how dimly it glows and read the brightness gauge (light meter, or sound bars for a buzzer).
Before adding a second cell in series, PREDICT out loud or in writing what will happen to the brightness and why, then add the cell and watch the filament glow harder and the gauge climb.
Add a third cell, predicting first each time, and record each result in a results strip: number of cells → brightness, taking a couple of readings so the pattern is your own finding.

Try the counter-case: add a cell but connect it the wrong way round (like terminal to like terminal) so it opposes the others. Predict first — does it get brighter? Observe that the bulb DIMS, and with two equal cells opposing it goes out, because the reversed cell pushes against the others.
Keep adding cells past the bulb's rating and watch it flash and blow, showing there is a sensible maximum.
Keep the bulb and wiring fixed throughout so only the number of cells changes — this builds the fair test in.
activities.title: Series-circuit playground: add a cell, predict the brightness

feedback: If a learner sorts purely by cell count and ignores a reversed cell: a flipped cell opposes the others, so counting cells alone is not enough — the direction of each push matters.

If a learner says any extra cell anywhere brightens the bulb: cells must add in series (same direction) to raise the push; two identical cells in parallel give about the same voltage as one, so do not raise brightness, and two equal cells facing opposite ways cancel each other's push.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can state and apply the pattern, recognise when a reversed cell or a parallel arrangement breaks it, and justify predictions in terms of push/energy rather than used-up current.
learnerActions: Order a set of 1-cell, 2-cell and 3-cell series circuits from dimmest to brightest and state the rule you used.
Answer prediction questions such as 'What happens to the brightness if you add a third cell in series?' and justify the answer with 'more push → more energy → brighter'.
Spot the circuit that breaks the trend because one of its cells is reversed, and explain why that circuit dims.
Predict and compare: two cells side by side (parallel) versus two in a line (series) — which gives a brighter bulb, and why?
